content: 1. Policies, standards, or guidelines must align with national standards. These can take the form of written policy documents, standard operating procedures, or clinical practice guidelines. 2. Indicate Yes if all staff conducting outpatient clinics have been oriented to or routinely use the relevant policies, standards, or guidelines. 3. To review sick-child outpatient clinics, examine the sick-child registers for a three-month period from the previous year. Count the total number of sick-child visits by diagnosis, ensuring that individual entries in facility registers are used rather than monthly summaries. 4. Compare child health data reported in the routine health management information system (HMIS) with facility register data for the same three-month period. Calculate a verification factor by dividing the direct register count by the count reported in the HMIS. This process validates reported data against facility records. If significant discrepancies are found, discuss potential reasons with facility staff. 5. To assess the training status of outpatient staff in child health, ask the facility or clinic manager to identify all staff working in infant and child health care. List staff by title and category, ensuring only currently active staff are included. Include new and trainee staff if they are currently working. 6. Inquire about the training received by staff in the past five years, categorized by type of training. Record Yes if training has been received, counting each type of training only once per staff member. Summarize findings by recording the total number of staff and the proportion trained by topic, as well as by staff category (e.g., doctor, nurse, medical assistant). 7. Consolidate findings from Checklists 1–7 onto a master set or flip charts. Review each checklist to identify strengths and areas for improvement. Additional areas for improvement not listed on the checklists can also be noted. 8. After discussion, agree on the two or three most critical areas for improvement to address in the next three months. For each area, identify underlying reasons for the observed gaps and propose actions to address them, specifying responsibilities and timelines. 9. Debrief with the facility director and staff to discuss and finalize the findings and action plan. Leave a copy of the Facility Priority Actions with the director and staff, and determine when the plan will be reviewed and who will be responsible for conducting the review. 10. If the assessment is part of an annual implementation review, retain Checklists 1–7 for review with the larger review team. 11. To synthesize findings from multiple facilities, create summary forms for Checklists 1–7 on flip-chart paper and post them on the wall. Record data for each facility in separate columns, adding extra columns if there are more than 18 facilities. 12. Summarize data for Checklists 4, 5, and 6 as follows: For Checklist 4, record Yes or No for all criteria met (e.g., availability and proper storage of medicines and supplies). For Checklist 5, record Yes if written policies are available and staff have been oriented. For Checklist 6, record the verification factor for each disease and month. 13. Calculate totals for each of the three main facility categories (national and regional hospitals, first-level referral hospitals, and first-level health facilities). Discuss indicators, marking low-performing ones with a red marker and those showing progress with a green marker. 14. Participants should walk through the checklist summary sheets as a group to identify strengths and priority areas for improvement. Discuss findings and reach consensus on the main findings. 15. Use findings to develop an annual implementation plan for improving child health. Identify priority problems by reviewing findings from checklists and monitoring and evaluation tables, including differences between facility levels. Summarize prioritized areas for improvement and ensure group consensus. 16. Develop an annual child health action plan by reviewing actions from the previous plan and brainstorming new actions to address priority areas. Base actions on the underlying reasons for gaps, considering the importance of improving child health clinical practice, resource availability, and feasibility within three months. 17. Write the agreed priority actions on flip-chart paper and ensure they are actionable within the specified timeframe.
